_README: Human adjudications that settle a queued ruling. The other half of rejections.json:
that file records 'do not publish', this one records 'a person read this and it is
fine'. Without it the review queue cannot shrink -- verify.py re-surfaces every
medium-confidence and flagged item on every run, so the same items get re-read forever
and the queue stops meaning anything.
An approval is scoped to the exact text and sources it was given. `signature` is
verify.py's fingerprint of (ruling text + cited comment ids + thread context) at review
time; if any of those change the approval lapses and the item returns to the queue. So
an approval cannot silence a ruling that was later rewritten, which is the whole risk of
a file like this.
Write `signature: null` to approve regardless of future edits. Do that only for a
finding about the *source* rather than the ruling -- e.g. 'this answer is terse because
the question carried the polarity, and that is correct here'.
verdict is one of:
approved   the ruling is faithful and well-sourced; the model's objection is wrong or moot
accepted   the objection is fair but the ruling is the best available; reason says why
A ruling that should change is not recorded here -- change it. A ruling that should go
is not recorded here either -- that is rejections.json.
The 30 `terse source` approvals dated 2026-08-30 all rest on the same evidence, and the
reason quotes it: the question the terse answer was replying to, recovered by walking
`parent` up the comment thread. A short answer's polarity lives in its question, so that
quote is the whole check -- read it against the ruling and the approval either holds or
it does not. Three items in that pass were not approved; the rulings were changed.

reason: Aaron asked: “When the rulebook says that all powers are optional, what exactly does that
mean for powers that affect other players? Take the osprey, for instance - its power is
that, when activated, all players gain a fish from the supply. But the power is optional!
Does that mean: a) the player who controls the osprey can - if they wish - choose not to
activate the osprey, resulting in nobody getting any fish or b) the osprey is always
activated, but every player can…”  Jamey Stegmaier answered: “(a) is correct :)”  The ruling
answers that question in that direction.
Approved as rewritten. Jamey's '(a) is correct' answers a two-option question, and
(a) is the owner declining to activate at all -- which is now the whole row. The
sentence about other players declining their [fish] was not in this thread; it is
20221121, promoted to a general ruling that reaches this card.

The verifier holds this at `overstated`/medium on the grounds that Jamey hedged twice
and never himself determined whether Spangled Drongo's power is scoped to the 'gain
food' action, so the ruling's flat 'by any means' clause is stronger than comment 42903
supports. That objection is accurate about 42903 and moot about the corpus: comment
109108 answers exactly that question ('does this mean that during a round a player gains
a nectar for any reason - not just gaining food' / 'it does mean what you described'),
and is listed in extra-citations.json. The verifier itself concedes the conclusion is
defensible on that basis.
Its remaining objection -- that 109108's once-between-turns point is dropped -- is
correct but not a defect here. That limit is published on Spangled Drongo's own card as
ruling 20241228. A player reading Red-Winged Parrot needs to know that a gift counts as
a gain; they do not need the Drongo's timing rule on the Parrot's page.
Keeping the verdict rather than forcing it to faithful: the model is reasoning correctly
from what it was given, and loosening the gate to make one item green would cost the
next inversion.
Faith Brown asked: “In the OE addition with the bonus card Site Selection Expert , how do
you score the Brown headed Cowbird? It does not have a nest on the card, but in real life
the bird lays eggs in other birds’ nests so we have a debate going as to if this would
qualify as star nest ability in the new expansion. Does it just not count or get counted as
a wild?”  Jamey Stegmaier answered: “It doesn't count. :)”  The ruling answers that question
in that direction.
The question offers both readings explicitly -- 'Does it just not count or get counted
as a wild?' -- so 'It doesn't count' picks one and the ruling states that one.

Stan Chechak asked: “Please provide a verification of our rule interpretation for the
Hunting and Fishing Powers birds in the Asian Expansion of Wingspan. For example, the Forest
Owlet (WHEN ACTIVATED: Choose any 2 DICE. Roll them up to 3 times. Each time, if you roll at
least 1 Invertebrate or Rodent, cache 1 here. If not, stop and return all food cached here
this turn.). Please verify that if there are only 2 DICE in the birdfeeder, and the owner of
the Forest Owlet chooses…”  Jamey Stegmaier answered: “That's correct, Stan!”  The ruling
answers that question in that direction.
The longest question in the corpus and the shortest answer. Stan spelled out the whole
sequence -- roll outside the feeder, then reroll all 5 to reset, then continue -- and
the ruling restates his sequence, so the terse 'That's correct, Stan!' is fully
licensed.

just one duet token per bird card so only one. Thanks!”  Jamey Stegmaier answered: “That's

PS asked: “When determining the number of birds with colour in their names for the bonus
card can the colour be part of a name, ie. silvereye?”  Jamey Stegmaier answered: “It can
indeed! :)”  The ruling answers that question in that direction.
Approved as rewritten. 'It can indeed!' answers 'can the colour be part of a name, ie.
silvereye?', which licenses the yes but not the old row's 'part of a larger word' --
read that way it contradicts Barred Owl and Baya Weaver. The rule Jamey actually
stated is compound words (comment 60794, now in extra-citations.json).
